A special master has ruled in Apple's favor in a dispute over Apple's bid to obtain documents from 14 federal agencies as part of its defense in an antitrust lawsuit. Here's what happened.

Background

Last May, Apple asked the court hearing the Department of Justice's 2024 antitrust case against it to order the following 14 federal agencies to turn over documents regarding how they evaluate, purchase, and use smartphones and wearables:

  • Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • Department of Commerce
  • Department of Homeland Security
  • Department of Defense
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • General Services Administration
  • Department of Labor
  • National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • National Security Agency (NSA)
  • Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • Office of Management and Budget
  • Office of Personnel Management
  • Department of State

In its request, Apple noted that those records could help it defend against allegations that its iPhone policies were anticompetitive in nature.

The short version is that Apple argued that if federal agencies select its products based on their security, privacy, or other features, that would help support its claim that the disputed practices are legitimate product advantages, not anticompetitive restrictions.

The government pushed back, however, arguing that the agencies are not parties to the case, don't regulate smartphones, and don't buy or use such products the same way regular consumers do.

The government asked the court to quash the subpoenas, claiming they were irrelevant and overly burdensome, and that they could implicate privileged, confidential, or national-security-sensitive material.

The court then referred the dispute to retired federal judge Jose Linares, who is serving as a special discovery master to decide whether Apple can enforce the subpoenas.

In complex cases involving heavy discovery, courts will sometimes appoint a special master to rule on narrower disputes to reduce the workload on the presiding judge. Special masters can be retired judges, practicing attorneys, or other experts with relevant experience.

Apple wins the right to obtain documents from federal agencies

Judge Linares has now ruled in Apple's favor, finding that all of its document requests are relevant to the core allegations in the case. He also found that the government failed to provide meaningful support for its broad objections.

From his ruling:

and

Although the special master ruled in Apple's favor, that doesn't mean Apple will immediately receive all of the documents it requested.

Instead, the agencies can still withhold specific records they consider privileged or otherwise protected, but they must identify them on a privilege log. Any disputes over those claims could trigger a new round of discovery fights, including possible in-camera review by Judge Linares.
